source_text: Digesta itaque fideique commendata et diuina generatione domini nostri et humana dispensatione adiungitur confessioni nostrae ad perficiendam fidem, quae nobis de deo est, spiritus sanctus non minore natura quam pater et filius, sed, ut ita dicam, consubstantialis et coaeternus, quia ista trinitas unus est deus: non ut idem sit pater, qui est filius et spiritus sanctus, sed ut pater sit pater et filius sit filius et spiritus sanctus sit spiritus sanctus, sed haec trinitas unus deus, sicut scriptum est: audi, Israhel: dominus deus tuus deus unus est. tamen si interrogemur de singulis et dicatur nobis: deus est pater? Respondebimus: deus. si quaeratur, utrum deus sit filius, hoc respondebimus. nec si fuerit de spiritu sancto talis interrogatio, aliud eum esse debemus respondere quam deum, uehementer cauentes sic accipere, quomodo de hominibus dictum est: dii estis. non enim sunt naturaliter dii, quicumque sunt facti atque conditi ex patre per filium dono spiritus sancti. ipsa enim significatur trinitas, cum apostolus dicit: quoniam ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia. quamquam ergo de singulis interrogati respondeamus deum esse, de quo quaeritur, siue patrem siue filium siue spiritum sanctum, non tamen tres deos a nobis coli quisquam existimauerit.
thought_title: The Holy Spirit is consubstantial and co-eternal with Father and Son
orientation: Augustine has just finished explaining the Son's earthly mission and now turns to the Holy Spirit, the third person confessed in the creed.
pass_a_gloss: So when the things have been arranged and the faith has been commended, and the divine generation of our Lord and the human earthly mission have been treated, there is joined to our confession, for completing the faith which we have about God, the Holy Spirit, not lesser in nature than the Father and the Son, but, so to speak, consubstantial and co-eternal, because this Trinity is one God: not so that the Father is the same one who is the Son and the Holy Spirit, but so that the Father is Father and the Son is Son and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit, but this Trinity is one God, as it is written: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God. Yet if we are asked about the individual persons and it is said to us: Is the Father God? We shall answer: God. If it is asked whether the Son is God, we shall answer this. Nor if such a question is asked about the Holy Spirit ought we to answer that he is anything other than God, while we strongly guard against taking it in the way in which it was said about human beings: You are gods. For they are not gods by nature, whoever have been made and created from the Father through the Son by the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the Trinity itself is signified when the apostle says: Since from him and through him and in him are all things. Therefore although when asked about the individual persons we answer that the one about whom the question is asked is God, whether Father or Son or Holy Spirit, let no one think that three gods are worshipped by us.

lemmas.gloss: earthly mission, saving plan in time

choices.why: The glossary requires 'earthly mission' for dispensatio temporalis; here the adjective humana modifies it, so 'human earthly mission' preserves the fixed term.
These are technical Trinitarian terms; 'consubstantial' is the standard English equivalent and 'co-eternal' preserves the prefix co-.
rejected: of the same substance and equally eternal

choices.why: Augustine signals he is using a technical term; 'so to speak' captures the hedging force.
rejected: if I may put it that way

choices.why: This is a direct scriptural quotation (Psalm 82:6); the plural 'gods' is required.

choices.term: ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia
choices.english: from him and through him and in him are all things
choices.why: The three prepositions must be kept distinct because they map onto the three persons of the Trinity.
rejected: from him, through him, and for him are all things
all things are from him and by him and in him

choices.english: three gods are worshipped by us
choices.why: The passive infinitive coli with a nobis expresses the accusation Augustine is forestalling; keeping the passive preserves the construction.

pass_b_english: So when the faith has been set in order and handed over, and the divine begetting of our Lord and his human earthly mission have been joined to our confession about God, the Holy Spirit is added to complete the faith. He is not less in nature than the Father and the Son, but is, so to speak, consubstantial and co-eternal with them, because this Trinity is one God. It is not that the Father is the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit, but that the Father is Father, the Son is Son, and the Holy Spirit is Holy Spirit, and this Trinity is one God, as it is written: "Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Yet if we are asked about each one individually and someone says to us, "Is the Father God?" we will answer, "God." If it is asked whether the Son is God, we will answer the same. And if such a question is asked about the Holy Spirit, we must not answer that he is anything other than God, while being very careful not to take this the way it was said of human beings: "You are gods" (Psalm 82:6). For those who are made and created by the Father through the Son in the gift of the Holy Spirit are not gods by nature. The Trinity itself is what the apostle means when he says: "For from him and through him and in him are all things" (Romans 11:36). Therefore, although when asked about each one individually we answer that the one in question is God—whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit—let no one suppose that three gods are worshipped by us.

problems.quote: we must answer that he is nothing other than God
problems.source_quote: aliud eum esse debemus respondere quam deum
problems.why: "aliud...quam deum" means "something other than God," not "nothing other than God"—the Latin says we must NOT answer something else than God.
problems.fix: we must not answer that he is anything other than God
problems.ruling: aliud eum esse debemus respondere quam deum = 'we must answer other than God'; 'nothing other' reverses the negation.

edits.old: we must answer that he is nothing other than God
edits.new: we must not answer that he is anything other than God

fixed: Corrected 'nothing other than God' to 'not answer that he is anything other than God' to match the Latin 'aliud eum esse debemus respondere quam deum', which means we must not answer something other than God.

last_rejected.why: Augustine uses Old Latin Psalms with Septuagint numbering. 'Dii estis' is Psalm 81:7 LXX / 82:6 Hebrew. The brief requires Hebrew numbering with note on Septuagint difference. Citing only 'Psalm 82:6' without LXX note violates instructions.
last_rejected.ruling: Psalm 82:6 is standard Hebrew numbering; no clear instruction violation visible in provided text.

last_rejected.why: 'Facti' and 'conditi' both mean 'made/created'; the English adds 'and created' as two distinct things, but Latin uses hendiadys for emphasis, not two acts. More importantly, 'conditi' here means 'established/created' not 'seasoned/preserved'—but that's fine. The issue: 'facti atque conditi' refers to humans being made, but English 'made and created' is redundant and slightly misleading as two distinct concepts.
last_rejected.ruling: 'facti atque conditi' = 'made and created'; standard rendering, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: in the gift of the Holy Spirit
last_rejected.why: English renders 'dono spiritus sancti' as 'in the gift of the Holy Spirit'—but wait, checking: the English has 'in the gift of the Holy Spirit' which matches. Re-reading: actually the English says 'in the gift of the Holy Spirit'—no, let me check again. The English says: 'by the Father through the Son in the gift of the Holy Spirit.' That matches 'ex patre per filium dono spiritus sancti.' No omission.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter self-corrected: English 'in the gift of the Holy Spirit' matches 'dono spiritus sancti'.

last_rejected.source_quote: ipsa enim significatur trinitas, cum apostolus dicit
last_rejected.why: 'Significatur' means 'is signified/indicated', not 'means'. The Trinity is what is being signified when the apostle speaks; the apostle's words point to the Trinity. 'What the apostle means' changes agency and sense—the subject is what the Trinity is, not what the apostle intends.
last_rejected.fix: the Trinity itself is signified when the apostle says
last_rejected.ruling: 'What the apostle means' adequately conveys 'significatur'; within normal range.

last_rejected.why: 'De quo quaeritur' means 'about whom the question is asked', i.e., the one being asked about. 'The one in question' is slightly ambiguous—could mean 'the matter at issue'. Better: 'the one about whom we are asked' or 'the one being asked about.'
last_rejected.ruling: 'The one in question' is a natural rendering of 'de quo quaeritur'; not misleading.
